confidence_note: The reference TR text says a 20-week yoga program gave 'most' chronic PTSD patients relief that drugs and talk therapy couldn't; the book describes an NIH-funded study of trauma-sensitive yoga for women with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD, compared against a control group, with the yoga group improving significantly more. The program length and exact percentages are not verified here and are omitted; 'most participants' and 'couldn't be achieved by drugs' are overstatements. The framing that van der Kolk noticed a common factor in non-recovering patients is a simplification of his broader argument that insight alone doesn't calm the nervous system.
facts: Van der Kolk argues that understanding why you feel threatened does not by itself stop the body from reacting as if it is under threat.
His Trauma Center studied trauma-sensitive yoga for women with chronic PTSD who had not improved with other treatments, comparing a weekly yoga class with a control group.
The yoga group showed significantly greater reductions in PTSD symptoms than the control group.
He explains the mechanism as learning to notice internal sensations safely (interoception), to regulate breathing, and to tolerate feelings in the body without being overwhelmed.
He also measured heart rate variability, a sign of how flexibly the nervous system responds, and presents yoga as one way to improve it.
The book describes other body-based and action-based approaches too, including theater programs, neurofeedback and EMDR, rather than presenting yoga as a single cure.
tension: People can gain real insight into their trauma in talk therapy and still have a nervous system that doesn't believe them.
opening_idea: Open with a room of women who had tried other treatments without relief, now asked simply to notice their breath and where they feel their feet.

lessons.idea: Insight and regulation are different kinds of change.
lessons.anchor: Van der Kolk argues understanding the cause does not stop the body's alarm.

lessons.idea: Noticing sensation safely is itself a skill.
lessons.anchor: The yoga work centered on interoception, breathing and tolerating sensations.

lessons.idea: Recovery can come from repeated experiences, not only explanations.
lessons.anchor: A weekly practice, not a single insight, produced improvement in the study.

reflect: Have you ever fully understood why something upset you, and still felt it just as strongly?
Where in your body do you tend to notice stress first?
reflect_final: The next time you feel tension build, spend a few breaths just noticing where it sits in your body before deciding what to do, and see whether anything shifts.

use_cases.situation: Before a difficult presentation, your chest tightens despite knowing you're prepared.
use_cases.move: Take a slow breath and notice your feet on the floor before the first slide, then check whether your voice feels steadier.

use_cases.situation: A friend says they've 'talked it all out' in therapy but still feel on edge.
use_cases.move: Mention that van der Kolk found understanding didn't always calm the body, and ask whether they'd want to try a gentle movement class together.

use_cases.situation: At the end of a stressful workday.
use_cases.move: Before opening your phone, pause for a minute to notice where you're holding tension, and note what you find.

pocket_idea: The women in van der Kolk's yoga study had already been told why they felt unsafe; what helped was learning, week by week, to feel their own body without alarm.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: For women with chronic PTSD who hadn't responded to other treatment, a weekly yoga class did better than the comparison group.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Van der Kolk's team offered trauma-sensitive yoga to women whose PTSD hadn't improved; focusing on breath and sensation, they improved significantly more than controls.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Have you ever noticed a physical activity calm you more than talking something through?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: From 'if I understand it, I'll feel better' to 'my body has to learn it's safe, too.'
